paper_title: OPMD: On-Policy Mechanism Distillation Beyond Output Supervision

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model by supervising a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy, but its supervision remains confined to the output space. Consequently, OPD transfers what a teacher predicts without supervising the intermediate computation that produces those predictions. Simply distilling intermediate representations like representation matching is insufficient since teacher and student representations may differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's subsequent computation. We introduce On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), which transfers teacher-derived intermediate computation while explicitly accounting for its compatibility with the student. OPMD first constructs a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states usable by the student's downstream computation, then it internalizes these states from on-policy trajectories. OPMD achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher--student settings, and generalizes to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning. Further analyses show that mechanism supervision yields more effective reasoning and meaningfully alters the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies, supporting that it transfers information beyond output supervision alone. Together, these results establish mechanism-level supervision as an effective way to move on-policy distillation beyond output supervision, enabling students to learn inner mechanisms they can use and internalize.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: On-policy distillation supervises student on textual prefixes sampled from its own policy, addressing key mismatch between training and deployment (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). However, agreement on observed next-token distributions does not establish agreement about how evidence is represented and transformed across layers. Models with similar next-token distributions can organize evidence differently in the representation space and rely on different computational pathways at depth (Belrose et al., 2025; Nikankin et al., 2025). Output-level agreement therefore does not uniquely determine the internal computation learned by the student. Here, textual prefixes serve as the states of the autoregressive decision process. We use latent states for the networks internal hidden representations. Output supervision constrains predictions but only indirectly constrains the latent states used to produce them. Particularly for complex reasoning tasks, output-level supervision may therefore leave valuable intermediate computational information untransferred (Jiao et al., 2020a; Sun et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; 2021). This raises natural question: can the latent states of stronger teacher provide actionable information that improves the students subsequent computation? Our preliminary analysis provides direct evidence that intermediate latent states contain actionable information for reasoning. We evaluate on AMC 2023 (LI et al., 2024) and use cross-model activation patching (Prakash et al., 2024), replacing the Base models hidden state at selected layer with the corresponding state from its RL-optimized counterpart while leaving all subsequent computation unchanged. As shown in Figure 1(a), patching latent states from an RL-optimized model into its base model substantially improves downstream Correspondence to Jingyi Yu, Quan Li, and Kan Ren.

sections.content: task accuracy, demonstrating that RL-optimized latent states contain task-relevant information that remains usable by the Base models downstream computation. However, simply transferring such information is non-trivial, especially when teacher and student have different hidden dimensions or representation geometries, typically requiring mapping between their representation spaces. Existing feature-based distillation methods therefore rely on manually specified layer correspondences, learned projections, or specially designed relational objectives to make their intermediate latent states comparable (Jiao et al., 2020a; Wang et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2023). We further extend cross-model activation patching to heterogeneous teacherstudent pairs by mapping the teachers latent state into the students hidden space. As shown in Figure 1(b), patching teacher latent states mapped by an MSE-trained projector can severely disrupt student generation, whereas states produced by task-trained projector yield substantial gains across patching depths. These results suggest that minimizing hidden-state reconstruction error is not sufficient to produce representations that the students downstream computation can use. What matters is therefore not only whether teacher latent state can be mapped close to student latent state, but whether the mapped latent state lies in form that is computationally usable by the students remaining layers. This motivates constructing teacher-informed latent states directly within the students computational interface. (a) (b) Figure 1: Teacher latent states and student compatibility. AMC accuracy under interventions at different depths. Motivated by these observations, we do not directly force the student to reproduce the teachers hidden states. Instead, we first construct student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher information into intermediate states optimized to improve the students downstream behavior and to be effectively used by its subsequent layers. These states then serve as richer computational targets for distillation. Concretely, learned bridge injects teacher hidden states into frozen student backbone, producing teacher-informed representations within the students own computational interface. We then perform on-policy internalization, training native student to reproduce these teacher-induced hidden trajectories on student-generated prefixes. At deployment, the teacher model and bridge are removed, leaving only the native student. This construction lets us test whether teacher-derived information becomes usable through the students own parameters. We evaluate OPMD on downstream reasoning tasks across three teacherstudent pairs, demonstrating gains over output-level OPD. We further extend the framework to multiple domain teachers and validate mechanism distillation through cross-family SFT without logit-level KL supervision. Layer-level interventions further reveal changes in how students approach problem, beyond changes in answer accuracy. In case study, intermediate-layer updates recover solution-route preferences closer to the fully distilled model, while substantial accuracy gap remains. These observations distinguish learning preferred solution strategy from realizing the computation needed to execute it successfully. Our contributions are threefold. First, we construct student-compatible teacher and train the native student to internalize its latent states through on-policy supervision. Second, we evaluate this framework across teacherstudent pairs, multiple domain teachers, and cross-family SFT. Third, we investigate whether different layer groups internalize different reasoning mechanisms, using their distinct solution-route preferences to examine how strategy selection relates to successful execution.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: On-policy language-model distillation. To mitigate exposure bias and distribution shift in autoregressive generation, on-policy distillation supervises the student on prefixes sampled from its own rollout policy (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024), with recent variants exploring alternative divergence formulations and token-level feedback allocation (Xu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Most existing methods operate through output-level teacher signals, improving where and how the student receives supervision without directly constraining its intermediate computation. Recent work has begun extending the on-policy paradigm to representation-level supervision (Yang et al., 2026a). OPMD similarly adopts student-generated prefixes, but focuses on constructing teacher-informed intermediate targets that can be effectively used by the students subsequent computation. Representation-based distillation. Intermediate supervision ranges from hidden-state and layerwise matching to attention and relational distillation (Romero et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2019; Jiao et al., 2020b; Wang et al., 2020; 2021; Liang et al., 2023). In reasoning models, OPRD aligns intermediate representations on student-generated trajectories, whereas PHF transfers hidden transitions and trajectory geometry from reference-conditioned privileged teacher (Yang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026b). These approaches demonstrate the value of intermediate supervision, but primarily define transfer through representational correspondence or trajectory matching, without explicitly ensuring that the resulting states can be effectively used by the students subsequent computation. OPMD addresses this distinction by constructing student-compatible intermediate targets before internalizing them into the native student. Latent Interventions and Internalization. Intermediate computation can be modified by externally supplied signals. Activation patching replaces internal states to measure their causal effect on subsequent computation, while learned conditioning architectures such as ControlNet inject additional information into frozen pretrained backbones through trainable control pathways (Heimersheim & Nanda, 2024; Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023). complementary line of work internalizes privileged or contextual information so that it is no longer required at inference time (Zhao et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026). OPMD combines these perspectives by using teacherconditioned intervention to construct useful intermediate targets and subsequently internalizing the resulting hidden trajectories into the native student.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate task performance, transfer across training settings, and the behavioral changes retained by weight patching. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide training hyperparameters, implementation details, and computational resources in Appendix A. We will release the code upon acceptance. 4.1 DOES ON-POLICY INTERNALIZATION IMPROVE DISTILLATION? We first test whether OPMD improves mathematical reasoning over output-level distillation across different teachers and students. Setting and baselines. Our main mathematical distillation experiments use DAPO-Math-17K (Yu et al., 2025) for training and AMC, AIME 2024 (LI et al., 2024), and AIME 2025 (Balunovic et al., 2026) for evaluation. The teachers are Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025) and Qwen3-4B-Non-ThinkingRL-Math (RL-Math) (Yang et al., 2026b). We use Qwen3-1.7B-Base (abbreviated as Qwen3-1.7B) and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (abbreviated as Qwen2.5-3B) (Qwen et al., 2025) as students in the main comparisons. The main comparisons are Qwen3-4B Qwen3-1.7B-Base, RL-Math Qwen31.7B-Base, and RL-Math Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct. Within each comparison, methods share the student initialization and training data and are evaluated at matched training steps. We compare against output-level OPD (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026a), SFT on teacher-generated responses, and OPRD-Bridge (Yang et al., 2026a), which uses frozen low-rank alignment for representation distillation across models. Evaluation protocol. The main mathematical comparisons report avg@16, the mean final-answer accuracy over 16 sampled responses per problem. The checkpoint analyses evaluate 40 AMC problems and 30 problems per AIME benchmark with temperature 0.7 and top-p = 0.95. Appendix specifies experiment-specific evaluation settings.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Figure 5: AMC accuracy versus training time (top) and FLOPs (bottom). OPMD costs include Stage and Stage II. We introduced On-policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), an on-policy distillation framework that moves beyond output supervision by explicitly transferring intermediate computation mechanisms. Our key observation is that directly matching teacher and student representations is not sufficient, geometric alignment does not guarantee that transferred states can be effectively used by the students subsequent computation. OPMD addresses this gap in two stages, it first constructs studentcompatible teacher by optimizing teacher-derived intermediate states for their downstream functional utility, and then internalizes these states on student-generated trajectories so that the resulting student operates independently at inference time. Across three teacher-student settings, OPMD significantly improves reasoning capability over output-level OPD, while also extending to multiteacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning. Further analyses show that these gains are accompanied by more effective reasoning at comparable or lower response cost, and that the internalized updates induce meaningful changes in intermediate computation and solution strategies rather than merely reproducing final outputs. Taken together, our results establish mechanism-level supervision as practical extension of on-policy distillation beyond output matching, and highlight computational compatibility and internalization as two key principles for transferring how stronger model reasons, not only what it predicts.

sections.title: LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our evaluation covers limited set of teacherstudent pairs and downstream tasks. Whether the observed gains extend to larger models, broader range of architectures, and tasks beyond mathematics and code generation remains to be tested. The two cases in Section 4.3 were selected for the OPMD students advantage over Patch 17 and do not establish general layer specialization or causal mechanisms.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work studies language-model distillation using existing mathematical reasoning and code benchmarks, with behavioral analysis conducted on model-generated responses. Distillation may transfer errors and biases from teachers, and improvements on these benchmarks do not establish reliability or safety in deployment. The route annotations are model-generated judgments and are interpreted as descriptive evidence, with disagreements and limitations reported in Appendix B.1.

Our on-policy experiments use only Lint on student-generated prefixes, without downstream task loss. For SFT+MD, we use the fixed weighted sum LSFT+MD = 0.5Lrep + LSFT. We first compared archived answer accuracy across problems and selected q17 and q22 because the OPMD student clearly outperformed Patch 17. The respective accuracies of the OPMD student and Patch 17 were 81.25% and 18.75% on q17, and 50.00% and 18.75% on q22. Only after selecting these cases did we inspect the responses and compare their solution routes. Patch 17 and Patch 814 patch the weights of blocks 1 to 7 and 8 to 14 from the step-1024 OPMD checkpoint into raw Qwen3-1.7B-Base. All other parameters remain those of the raw student. We retain all 16 archived responses per model and problem, including incorrect and incomplete outputs. Accuracy follows the original final-answer grader and does not certify the correctness of each reasoning step. Interpreting the routes. The identifiers q17 and q22 refer to archived examples rather than official AMC topic labels. The shared terms direct route and mediated route summarize the existing problem-specific labels rather than introduce new annotation task. For q17, the problem asks for the number of decimal digits in 85 510 155. The direct route maps to direct place value and uses decimal expansion, trailing zeros, or place-value relationships to obtain the digit count without logarithmic calculation. The mediated route maps to logarithm, where log10 + 1 or an equivalent logarithmic procedure supplies the adopted digit count. This includes balancing post-transfer quantities and conservation equations written directly in the transfer variable. It does not rely on separately derived value of the common final state as the intermediate input that produces the transfer amount. - target_mediated: The response first actually derives value for the common final state, then uses that value in difference or equation to infer the required transfer. Computing target only after the transfer as check is not target_mediated. Computing an average but abandoning it and then solving transfer constraint is direct_constraint. Conversely, an incorrect target used to calculate the transfer remains target_mediated.
